newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Small crowds greet Romanian king, patriarch.
newsitem.headline: Small crowds greet Romanian king, patriarch.

text.p: Romania's exiled King Michael was hailed by the head of the Orthodox church on Sunday as a son of the nation, but only small crowds turned out for a service in a homecoming no longer generating passion among Romanians.

Michael, forced to abdicate by pro-Moscow communists in 1947, is making his second trip back to his homeland after the new centrist government restored his citizenship last week and he agreed to abide by the 1991 republican constitution.

Patriarch Teoctist said the king had seen his church survive five decades of repression, the bulldozing of churches by dictator Nicolae Ceausescu and a 1987 attempt to pull down its headquarters, the 18th century Church of the Patriarchate.

"You are the son of our church and of our nation," the white-clad patriarch told Michael, seated in a gilded throne in the church spared from Ceausescu's destruction of one-fifth of central Bucharest to make way for a vast palace.
"God gave us strength to resist those chilling moments in 1987. We no longer have exiles. For us, for the church, we hope that you will gather our brothers in Europe around the church."

Outside the church, a crowd of no more than 3,000 people greeted the king. Some waved banners depicting "Greater Romania," including territories populated by ethnic Romanians and now part of Ukraine, Moldova and Bulgaria.
Michael was greeted on Bucharest streets after his arrival on Friday from exile in Switzerland by 20,000 well-wishers.
The authorities and many Romanians view the visit as yet another sign that the country is returning to normal after seven years of post-communist uncertainty.

There has been little of the drama of his first return in 1992, when hundreds of thousands pushed into the streets for a glimpse of the monarch. The king, 75, has appeared moved but somewhat overwhelmed and weary during the visit.
"This is a fine, sunny Sunday," said Christian Danciulescu, on his way to a stroll in a central Bucharest park. "He is a Romanian citizen now. Why should we be impressed?"

Ex-communist Ion Iliescu, president from Ceausescu's 1989 demise until his election defeat last November, had blocked attempts to return home over the past five years and insisted he be treated as a foreign commoner.
Opinion polls show a tiny fraction of Romanians, faced with plunging living standards in the transition to a market economy, favour restoration of the monarchy.

New centrist President Emil Constantinescu says the king's prestige could be put to use promoting Romania's foremost foreign policy goal -- early admission to NATO alongside favourites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
Michael has expressed willingness to assume this role, but members of his retinue say he should be "champion" of Romanian interests rather than ambassador, "a term unfit for a king".
Many of the king's engagements have been broadcast live, but some newspapers have been sceptical about their impact.

"A pale reception for a tired and disoriented Michael I," the independent daily Adevarul said in a weekend headline. The mass circulation Evenimentul Zilei put the story below sackings in Romania's police hierarchy - part of the government's drive to stamp out corruption.
Michael's five-day visit includes a visit on Monday to royal tombs northwest of the capital and a dinner with Constantinescu on Tuesday.
